title: Talking about your work
subtitle: What do you do? My job involves ...
summary: Say what job you do, explain what it involves, and talk about pay, hours and working conditions.

lesson.heading: What do you do?
lesson.text: People can ask about your job in different ways, and you can answer in different ways too. All of these questions mean the same thing.

examples.text: *A:* **What do you do?** *B:* I work in sales / marketing / a bank.
*A:* **What do you do for a living?** *B:* I'm a doctor / a hairdresser.
*A:* **What's your job?** *B:* I work for Union Bank / Fiat / Sony.

lesson.note: We say I work in + an area of work, but I work for + the name of a company.

lesson.heading: What does that involve?
lesson.text: **What does your job involve?** means 'What do you have to do exactly?'. James and Emma are business **consultants**: people who help others in a particular area. They advise people who want to **set up** (start) a business.

examples.note: = does the work in marketing; handle means the same
= in control of; in charge of means the same

examples.text: My job **involves** a lot of travel.

lesson.heading: Running a small team
lesson.text: Amy is a manager in a veterinary surgery. She **runs** (organises or controls) the **day-to-day** business of the surgery and is **in charge of** a small team. Her work involves a lot of **admin**, which is short for administration.

examples.text: She **runs** the day-to-day business of the surgery.
She is **in charge of** three receptionists, an accounts manager and a secretary.

examples.note: to complain = to say that something is wrong or not satisfactory

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.text: Three small words cause a lot of trouble. **Work** is uncountable, the verb is **advise** but the noun is **advice**, and **involve** is followed by *-ing*, not *to*.

examples.text: I have a lot of **work** to do.

lesson.heading: salary or wages?

left.label: salary
left.text: Money paid to professional people and office workers, usually paid into a bank account every month.
examples: Doctors and teachers are paid a **salary**.
My **salary** goes into my bank account on the 28th.

right.label: wages
right.text: Money usually paid for each hour, day or week of work to people who do more physical jobs.
examples: Builders and cleaners are often paid **wages**.
There is a **minimum wage**: employers cannot pay less than this.

lesson.note: Your income is the total amount of money you receive in a year, from one job or from two.

lesson.heading: Pay and income tax
lesson.text: Most workers are **paid** every month. Some of your **income** you can keep, but some goes to the government. In the UK this is called **income tax**.

examples.note: make is also possible: I make about £25,000 a year.

examples.text: I lose 20% of my income in **income tax**.

lesson.heading: Conditions
lesson.text: **Conditions** are the situation in which people work. Most people work **fixed hours**, e.g. 9 am to 5.30 pm; we often call this a **nine-to-five job**. Other people have to **do overtime**, which means work extra hours.

examples.text: It's not a **nine-to-five** job: I often work until eight.
Some people get paid for **overtime**; others don't.
examples.note: you can do overtime or work overtime

examples.text: Some people have good **working conditions**, e.g. nice offices and paid holidays.
New mothers and fathers get extra **time off** when a baby is born.
examples.note: time off = time when you are not at work

lesson.text: Remember the pair: the verb is *advise* (She advises me) but the noun is *advice* (She gives me advice).

exercises.prompt: Which of these words are directly connected with money?
Match each verb or phrase on the left with the words that go with it.
'I'm a marketing assistant.' Another way to say this is: I work ___ marketing.
exercises.explanation: We work in an area of work: in marketing, in sales, in a bank.

exercises.prompt: 'I'm employed by the government.' Another way to say this is: I work ___ the government.
exercises.explanation: We work for an employer or a company.

exercises.prompt: 'What do you have to do exactly?' Another way to ask this is: What does your job ___?
exercises.explanation: What does your job involve? asks what the work actually is.

options: My job involves reading government reports.
My job involves to read government reports.
My job involve reading government reports.
My job involves read government reports.
exercises.explanation: After involve we use a noun or an -ing form, never to + verb.

exercises.prompt: 'I advise clients.' Another way to say this is: My job involves giving ___ to clients.
exercises.explanation: The verb is advise, but the noun is advice.

exercises.prompt: 'I complained about the service.' Another way to say this is: I made a ___ about the service.
exercises.explanation: We make a complaint, and other people handle or deal with complaints.

exercises.prompt: Alexander is a regional manager, and he's ___ for a small team of five sales people.
exercises.explanation: To be responsible for something means to be in control of it.

exercises.prompt: He's in contact with his team on a day-to-___ basis.
It's not a nine-to-___ job: Alexander has to do a lot of overtime.
exercises.explanation: A nine-to-five job has fixed hours, e.g. 9 am to 5 pm.

exercises.prompt: After income ___ he makes £60,000 a year.
exercises.hint: (the money that goes to the government)
exercises.explanation: Income tax is the part of your income that goes to the government.

exercises.statement: Kelly works fixed hours - 9 am to 5 pm - and she doesn't have to do overtime.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Fixed hours are always the same, and overtime means extra hours.

exercises.statement: I have a lot of works to do this week.
exercises.explanation: Work is uncountable here: I have a lot of work to do this week.
